To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have identified eight putative type II TA modules in B. pseudomallei and that five of these are in genome islands.

the type II TA systems of B. pseudomallei are widely distributed in the genome and are located mainly in genome islands, and that the candidate toxins RelE1, RelE2, HipA and HicA can inhibit growth of the model host E. coli.
the genome of B. pseudomallei contains a total of 8 candidate type II TA systems, 5 of which are located in genome islands, and 4 of which are functional.

the identification of type II TA systems in B. pseudomallei and their characterization in vitro.

B.  pseudomallei has a diverse set of TA systems that are potentially involved in a number of cellular processes.
the TA systems in B. pseudomallei have the potential to cause growth inhibition, but that the effects are not as dramatic as in E. coli.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the B. psuedomallei TA modules are not essential for growth in vitro and that the TA systems may play a role in controlling the bacterial population.

the B. pseudomallei genome contains at least eight TA loci that can be divided into two groups: those with a RelE-like toxin (BPSS1060, BPSS1584 and BPSS0390) and those with a HicA-like toxin (BPSP0175, BPSP0176, BPSP0177, BPSP0178 and BPSP0179).
RelE1, RelE2, HicA and HipA are the most promising candidate toxins and their cognate antitoxic proteins are the most likely candidates as antitoxins.
The main takeaway from our work is that
B. pseudomallei has a diverse set of TA systems, some of which may be useful in the development of new antimicrobials.
B. pseudomallei contains a number of type II TA systems that are likely to play important roles in the biology of the organism.
TA systems are widely distributed amongst bacteria and are likely to play important roles in bacterial physiology.
